script.opening: "I’m worried about Mia — she keeps getting these attacks of really bad tummy pain in the middle of her tummy, lasting hours, where she goes pale, feels sick, sometimes vomits, and just wants to lie down. Then it passes and she’s totally back to normal for weeks. The GP did some tests and they were normal. I get migraines myself. What is it, and why do the tests keep coming back fine?"

facts.text: Mother, Rachel, on the phone. Mia (8) is at school today and well.

For about a year, every 3–5 weeks. Always the same: dull pain around the belly button, goes very pale with dark rings under her eyes, feels sick, vomits once or twice, off her food, wants to lie in a dark quiet room. Lasts 3–12 hours. Sleep helps.
Completely normal — "you’d never know". Eating well, playing football, no tummy aches in between.

Vomit never green, no blood. No blood in stools; bowels daily, soft. No weight loss — growing out of clothes normally. Never woken at night by pain. No fevers, no rashes, no joint pains, no mouth ulcers. Pain never on one side. No pain or burning passing urine. No headaches she complains of.
Often after a late night, a long car journey, or a missed breakfast. One attack the day before a school play.
Had blood tests at the surgery 2 months ago ("all normal, including the coeliac one"). Not sure if a urine test was done. No medicines; gives Calpol in attacks. No allergies. Born at term, healthy.
Rachel has migraine with aura; Mia’s grandma too. Lives with Mum, Dad and a brother (5). Happy at school, no bullying Rachel knows of.

Worried, a bit frustrated that "nothing is being found". Ask "But why are the tests normal?" and "Will she grow out of it?". Relieved to hear it is a recognised condition. Happy to keep a diary and bring Mia in to be weighed, measured and examined.

ice.ideas: "I keep thinking something’s being missed because the tests are normal."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a school friend’s sister had appendicitis "that the GP missed", and Rachel is scared of the same; also feels guilty that Mia might have "got my migraines".
ice.expectations: "To know what it is — maybe a scan or a referral to a specialist."

cues: "She’s totally back to normal for weeks" — well between attacks, which supports the diagnosis.
"I get migraines myself" — the family history.
"Why do the tests keep coming back fine?" — explain that normal tests support the diagnosis.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ABDOMINAL MIGRAINE — recurrent stereotyped central abdominal pain with pallor/nausea/vomiting/anorexia/lethargy lasting hours, with complete wellness between episodes, normal growth and often a migraine history
Understands it is largely a CLINICAL diagnosis of EXCLUSION and explains that NORMAL investigations SUPPORT (not undermine) the diagnosis

Screens the RED FLAGS that would not fit (weight loss/faltering growth, nocturnal/waking or persistent vomiting, bilious vomiting as an emergency, GI bleeding, fever, localised/RIF pain, abnormal exam, dysuria, symptoms between attacks) and arranges a face-to-face examination with growth and urine
Considers the differential (constipation, UTI, coeliac, IBD, surgical causes, functional abdominal pain) and uses appropriate basic tests (coeliac serology, urine) to exclude

Manages — reassurance/explanation, trigger identification/avoidance, lifestyle, acute symptomatic treatment (early paracetamol/ibuprofen per BNFC; no routine antiemetics under MHRA restrictions; no triptans at 8), and paediatric referral for frequent/severe episodes — with a symptom diary
Reassures and explains the diagnosis clearly (a real form of migraine, not "nothing"), addressing the "why are the tests normal?" concern, and checks understanding
Draws out and addresses the worry that something serious has been missed, explaining the safety-net and review plan so the parent feels heard rather than dismissed with ‘the tests are normal’

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review/reassessment, trigger/acute management, review and a diary, and paediatric referral if frequent/severe or red flags — recognising the pattern, not endlessly re-investigating

worked.txt: "What you’re describing — stereotyped attacks of central tummy pain with pallor and sickness lasting hours, then completely well for weeks, with your own migraines in the background — sounds like abdominal migraine. It’s a recognised form of migraine in children, and it’s real, not ‘nothing’."

"That’s exactly why the tests keep coming back normal — it’s a diagnosis we make from the pattern after ruling out other causes, not something a blood test shows. Normal results actually fit and are reassuring."

"Let me just check a few things that would make me think differently: is she losing weight or off her growth? Does the pain or vomiting wake her at night, is the vomit ever green, any blood in her stool or vomit, fevers, or pain always in one spot? … None of those — reassuring. I can’t examine her over the phone, though, so I’d like to see her in person to examine her tummy, check her height and weight on her growth chart, and test a urine sample."
"I’ll make sure constipation, a urine infection and coeliac have been considered, as those can mimic it — a urine test and a coeliac blood test if not done."

"For attacks: rest in a quiet, dark room, sips of fluid, and paracetamol or ibuprofen early in the attack. Anti-sickness medicines aren’t routinely used at her age, and migraine tablets like triptans aren’t licensed for her. Keep a diary to spot triggers — stress, missed meals, poor sleep, dehydration. If they’re frequent or disabling, I’d involve a paediatrician, who can decide about preventive options."

"If she ever vomits green, call 999 or go to A&E — that’s an emergency. Come back — or seek urgent help — if the pattern changes, she loses weight, the pain stays in one place or wakes her, you see blood, or she’s unwell between attacks. Otherwise this often improves with age, sometimes turning into ordinary migraines later."

f.learning: ABDOMINAL MIGRAINE is a recognised paediatric variant of migraine: recurrent, STEREOTYPED episodes of moderate-to-severe MIDLINE/central abdominal pain lasting hours (ICHD-3, international: 2–72 hours untreated; Rome IV, international: at least 1 hour) with associated PALLOR, nausea/vomiting, anorexia and lethargy, and — crucially — COMPLETE wellness between episodes with normal growth, often with a personal/family history of migraine, typically resolving or evolving into typical migraine in later childhood/adolescence. It is largely a CLINICAL diagnosis of EXCLUSION, made after history/examination and exclusion of red flags and other causes — which is why investigations are normal: normal tests SUPPORT rather than undermine the diagnosis, and explaining this prevents the family feeling nothing has been found. Screen the RED FLAGS (Rome IV alarm features) that would not fit abdominal migraine: weight loss/faltering growth, pain or vomiting waking the child from sleep/nocturnal symptoms, bilious vomiting (an emergency — possible malrotation/obstruction) or persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, chronic severe diarrhoea, fever, persistent right-sided/localised pain, abnormal examination, dysuria, joint/perianal/systemic features, family history of IBD, or symptoms between attacks — any of which warrant assessment/investigation. On the telephone, arrange a face-to-face review to examine her, plot growth and test urine. Consider the differential for recurrent paediatric abdominal pain (constipation, UTI, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, surgical causes such as intermittent obstruction/intussusception, intermittent pelviureteric junction obstruction, cyclical vomiting syndrome, mesenteric adenitis, and functional abdominal pain/IBS) and use appropriate basic tests (coeliac serology per NICE NG20, urine per NICE NG224; constipation per NICE CG99) to exclude. Manage with reassurance and clear explanation (a real form of migraine, not "nothing"), trigger identification/avoidance (stress, sleep, food, dehydration), lifestyle measures, acute symptomatic treatment (rest in a quiet dark room, early paracetamol or ibuprofen per BNFC, hydration; antiemetics are not routine at this age — domperidone not licensed under 12, MHRA December 2019; metoclopramide restricted in under-18s, MHRA August 2013 — and triptans are not licensed at 8), a symptom diary, and paediatric referral for frequent or severe episodes (preventive medicines are a specialist decision). The skill is recognising the stereotyped episodic pattern with symptom-free intervals, explaining why normal tests fit, excluding red flags, and managing/reassuring — not endless re-investigation.

knowledge.guideline: [1] International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition, 1.6.1.2 Abdominal migraine (International Headache Society 2018, international) · [2] Rome IV childhood functional gastrointestinal disorders, Hyams et al., Gastroenterology 2016 (international) · [3] NICE NG20 Coeliac disease (2015) · [4] NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) · [5] NICE CG99 Constipation in children and young people (2010) · [6] MHRA Drug Safety Update: domperidone (December 2019) and metoclopramide (August 2013)
knowledge.summary: Stereotyped attacks of central abdominal pain lasting hours, with pallor, nausea, vomiting or anorexia, complete wellness between attacks, normal growth and a family history of migraine fit abdominal migraine. It is a clinical diagnosis made once alarm features are absent and the examination, growth and simple tests are normal; normal tests support it. On the phone, take the history and red flags, then arrange a face-to-face review to examine her, plot growth and check urine. Manage with explanation, a diary, triggers, and early simple analgesia for attacks. Antiemetics and triptans are restricted at her age, and prevention is a paediatric decision.

points.t: ICHD-3 [1]: at least five attacks of midline, periumbilical or poorly localised dull pain of moderate or severe intensity, with at least two of anorexia, nausea, vomiting and pallor, lasting 2–72 hours untreated, and complete freedom from symptoms between attacks. Rome IV [2] uses episodes of at least 1 hour occurring at least twice in 6 months, stereotyped and incapacitating, separated by weeks to months.

Features that do not fit and need investigation [2]: weight loss or slowing of growth, gastrointestinal blood loss, significant vomiting (bilious, protracted or projectile), chronic severe diarrhoea, persistent right-sided pain, unexplained fever, pain or vomiting that wakes the child, dysuria, joint or perianal problems, family history of inflammatory bowel disease, abnormal examination, or symptoms between attacks.

Constipation [5], urinary tract infection [4], coeliac disease (NG20 [3]: offer serological testing to children with persistent unexplained abdominal symptoms or faltering growth), inflammatory bowel disease, intermittent obstruction such as malrotation (bilious vomiting is an emergency), intermittent pelviureteric junction obstruction (episodic flank pain and vomiting), cyclical vomiting syndrome, and functional abdominal pain.

Rest in a quiet, dark room, sips of fluid, and paracetamol or ibuprofen early in the attack, dose per BNFC. Domperidone is no longer licensed for children under 12 (MHRA 2019) and metoclopramide is restricted in under-18s (MHRA 2013) [6], so antiemetics are not routine in primary care. Triptans are not licensed at her age.

Regular meals, sleep and hydration, and a diary to identify triggers. If attacks are frequent or disabling, refer to a paediatrician; preventive medicines have limited evidence in children and are a specialist decision.

Attacks often lessen with age, and many children with abdominal migraine go on to have typical migraine headaches later. Explaining this, and that normal tests support the diagnosis, reduces repeated investigation.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Khan calling from the surgery. Am I speaking to Mia’s mum? Is now a good time to talk, and is Mia with you?
model.why: Confirms identity and setting on the telephone

model.text: Yes, it’s her mum. She’s fine at the moment. I’m worried about her though. She keeps getting these attacks of really bad pain in the middle of her tummy, lasting hours. She goes pale, feels sick, sometimes vomits, and just wants to lie down. Then it passes and she’s totally back to normal for weeks. The GP did some tests and they were normal. I get migraines myself. What is it, and why do the tests keep coming back fine?
That’s a really clear description. I’ll ask some questions to be sure nothing is being missed, and then I’ll explain what I think is going on.
Can you take me through the last attack from start to finish? Where exactly is the pain, and how long does it last?
Always around her belly button. It lasts a few hours, sometimes most of the day.
How often do they come, and are they all much the same? How much do they stop her doing things?
Every few weeks. They’re always the same. She has to lie down; she can’t do anything.
Between attacks, is she completely well? Eating normally, no tummy ache at all, normal energy?
model.why: Complete wellness between attacks: key criterion

model.text: Completely normal. You’d never know.
Now a few things that would make me think differently. Is the sick ever green or yellow-green? Any blood in her sick or her poo?
No, never green. No blood.
Has she lost weight, or dropped behind in height compared with her friends? Any fevers with the attacks? Does pain ever wake her at night?
No. She’s growing fine, I think. No temperatures. It doesn’t wake her.
Is the pain ever mainly on one side or low on the right? Any pain passing urine, weeing more, diarrhoea, or problems opening her bowels?
model.why: Localised pain, urinary and bowel symptoms: UTI, constipation, IBD

model.text: No, it’s always in the middle. Her bowels and wee seem normal.
Any headaches, or does light bother her during an attack? Any rashes, sore joints, mouth ulcers, or anyone in the family with bowel disease or coeliac disease?
model.why: Migraine features; systemic and family red flags

model.text: I haven’t noticed headaches. She just wants to lie down in a quiet room. Nothing else that I know of.
Do you know which tests were done?
I’m not sure exactly. Some blood tests, I think.
What have you been thinking it might be? And what worries you most?
I keep thinking something’s being missed because the tests are normal. I want to know what it is.

That’s a very natural worry. From what you’ve told me, this fits a condition called abdominal migraine. It’s a form of migraine that shows itself as tummy pain in children, often in families where a parent has migraine. It’s real, not ‘nothing’, and not in her head.
But why are the tests normal?

Because there’s no blood test for migraine. We make the diagnosis from this very typical pattern, once we’ve checked there are no warning signs. So normal tests actually fit with it and are reassuring. None of the warning signs I asked about are there.
model.why: Explains why normal tests support the diagnosis

model.text: I can’t examine her on the phone, so I’d like to see her in person this week: to feel her tummy, check her height and weight on a growth chart, and test a urine sample. If the coeliac blood test hasn’t been done, we’ll do it then.
model.why: Face-to-face examination, growth, urine; coeliac serology (NG20)

model.text: Okay, that would make me feel better.

For attacks: let her rest in a quiet, dark room with sips of fluid, and give paracetamol or ibuprofen at the right dose for her age early in the attack. Anti-sickness medicines aren’t routinely used at her age, and migraine tablets aren’t licensed for children as young as eight.
model.why: Acute treatment within licensing and MHRA advice

model.text: Please keep a diary of each attack: the date, what she ate, sleep, school stress, anything that went before. Regular meals, good sleep and plenty of fluid help. If attacks become frequent or are stopping her going to school, I’d ask a children’s doctor about preventive treatment.
I can do the diary. Will she grow out of it?
Often they settle as children get older, though some go on to have ordinary migraine headaches, like you.

Please get urgent help if she ever vomits green, has blood in her sick or poo, the pain stays in one place or doesn’t ease, she has a high temperature, she’s not herself between attacks, or she loses weight. Green vomit or severe pain that won’t settle means ringing 999 or going to A&E. Can you tell me the plan back?
model.why: Specific red-flag safety-net with routes; teach-back

model.text: Bring her in this week for a check and a urine test, dark room, painkillers early, a diary, and get help straight away for green sick, blood, pain in one place, fever or if she’s unwell between attacks.
That’s it exactly. I’ll book her in now.

social.t: Attacks can cause missed school. A short letter explaining the diagnosis and a plan for attacks at school can help.
The mother’s own migraine gives her understanding of triggers and can be used in explanation.

legal.t: Domperidone is licensed only for 12 and over weighing at least 35 kg (MHRA 2019). Off-label use in children is a specialist decision, made with informed consent.

professional.t: Abdominal pain in a child should not be diagnosed without examination; convert to face-to-face when examination is needed.
Repeated tests without a clear question increase anxiety and cost. Explain the rationale for the tests you do order.

community.t: Migraine charities provide information on childhood migraine and its variants, and school health teams can support attendance.

redFlags: Bilious (green) vomiting: possible malrotation or obstruction, emergency
Fever, nocturnal waking, localised or right-sided pain
Symptoms between attacks, dysuria, joint or perianal problems, family history of IBD or coeliac disease
ice: Concern: tests normal but attacks continue

playbook.diagnosis: “This fits abdominal migraine: a form of migraine in children that causes attacks of tummy pain rather than headache.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s the same switch in the nervous system that causes your migraines, but in children it often shows up in the tummy. Between attacks the body is completely normal, which is why the tests are normal too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something had been missed because the tests were normal. Normal tests actually fit this diagnosis.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her worry; support school attendance; involve the mother’s migraine experience.

Paediatric referral if frequent or disabling
safetyNet: Green vomit or severe unrelenting pain: 999 or A&E
Blood, fever, localised pain, weight loss, unwell between attacks: urgent review

pitfalls.intro: A telephone case where the diagnosis is recognisable from the history. Marks go to screening alarm features, arranging an examination, explaining why normal tests fit, and treating attacks within licensing.

items.why: Growth, abdominal findings and urine must be checked in a child.

items.fail: Missing bilious vomiting and growth questions.
items.why: Malrotation and organic disease must be excluded.
items.fix: Ask specifically about green vomit, blood, weight and growth.
Rest, fluids and early simple analgesia; paediatric advice if needed.

items.why: Adds anxiety without a clear question.
items.fix: Targeted tests: urine and coeliac serology if not done.

items.fail: “The tests are normal, so it’s nothing.”
items.fix: Explain that normal tests support abdominal migraine.

items.why: Parents need to know which signs are emergencies.
items.fix: Name green vomit, blood, fixed pain, fever and being unwell between attacks, with routes.

wordPics.fail: Orders another round of tests without a clear question; dismisses it because the tests are normal; misses bilious vomiting or growth questions; prescribes an antiemetic outside MHRA advice; diagnoses without ever examining her.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the stereotyped pattern, screens alarm features, explains the diagnosis, arranges an examination with growth and urine, and gives attack advice and a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains exactly why normal tests support the diagnosis; checks which tests were done and adds coeliac serology if needed; respects antiemetic and triptan restrictions; uses a diary with a clear paediatric referral threshold; gives an honest prognosis linked to the mother’s migraine.

avoid.dont: “The tests are normal, so there’s nothing wrong.”
avoid.instead: “There’s no test for migraine, so normal results actually fit and are reassuring.”
avoid.why: Dismissal leaves the parent feeling unheard and drives repeated attendance.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give her something for the sickness.”
avoid.instead: “Anti-sickness medicines aren’t routinely used at her age; rest, fluids and early painkillers help most.”
avoid.why: Domperidone is not licensed under 12 and metoclopramide is restricted in under-18s (MHRA).

avoid.dont: “Let’s repeat all the bloods to be sure.”
avoid.instead: “I’d like to examine her and check her growth and urine, and add a coeliac test if it hasn’t been done.”
avoid.why: Targeted assessment is safer and more useful than repeating normal tests.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition, 1.6.1.2 Abdominal migraine (International Headache Society 2018, international) · [2] Rome IV childhood functional gastrointestinal disorders, Hyams et al., Gastroenterology 2016 (international) · [3] NICE NG20 Coeliac disease (2015) · [4] NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) · [5] NICE CG99 Constipation in children and young people (2010) · [6] MHRA Drug Safety Update: domperidone (December 2019) and metoclopramide (August 2013)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Stereotyped attacks of central abdominal pain lasting hours, with pallor, nausea, vomiting or anorexia, complete wellness between attacks, normal growth and a family history of migraine fit abdominal migraine. It is a clinical diagnosis made once alarm features are absent and the examination, growth and simple tests are normal; normal tests support it. On the phone, take the history and red flags, then arrange a face-to-face review to examine her, plot growth and check urine. Manage with explanation, a diary, triggers, and early simple analgesia for attacks. Antiemetics and triptans are restricted at her age, and prevention is a paediatric decision.

points.t: ICHD-3 [1]: at least five attacks of midline, periumbilical or poorly localised dull pain of moderate or severe intensity, with at least two of anorexia, nausea, vomiting and pallor, lasting 2–72 hours untreated, and complete freedom from symptoms between attacks. Rome IV [2] uses episodes of at least 1 hour occurring at least twice in 6 months, stereotyped and incapacitating, separated by weeks to months.

Features that do not fit and need investigation [2]: weight loss or slowing of growth, gastrointestinal blood loss, significant vomiting (bilious, protracted or projectile), chronic severe diarrhoea, persistent right-sided pain, unexplained fever, pain or vomiting that wakes the child, dysuria, joint or perianal problems, family history of inflammatory bowel disease, abnormal examination, or symptoms between attacks.

Constipation [5], urinary tract infection [4], coeliac disease (NG20 [3]: offer serological testing to children with persistent unexplained abdominal symptoms or faltering growth), inflammatory bowel disease, intermittent obstruction such as malrotation (bilious vomiting is an emergency), intermittent pelviureteric junction obstruction (episodic flank pain and vomiting), cyclical vomiting syndrome, and functional abdominal pain.

Rest in a quiet, dark room, sips of fluid, and paracetamol or ibuprofen early in the attack, dose per BNFC. Domperidone is no longer licensed for children under 12 (MHRA 2019) and metoclopramide is restricted in under-18s (MHRA 2013) [6], so antiemetics are not routine in primary care. Triptans are not licensed at her age.

Regular meals, sleep and hydration, and a diary to identify triggers. If attacks are frequent or disabling, refer to a paediatrician; preventive medicines have limited evidence in children and are a specialist decision.

Attacks often lessen with age, and many children with abdominal migraine go on to have typical migraine headaches later. Explaining this, and that normal tests support the diagnosis, reduces repeated investigation.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirms identity and setting; lets the mother describe the attacks fully.
Impact on school and family; the mother’s own migraine and worry.
Picks up maternal migraine and the need to lie down as supportive cues; clarifies which tests were done.
Idea (something missed), concern (normal tests), expectation (a diagnosis).
Face-to-face review to examine, plot growth and test urine; coeliac serology if not done (NG20).
Abdominal migraine versus constipation, UTI, coeliac disease, IBD, intermittent obstruction, PUJ obstruction and cyclical vomiting.
Bilious vomiting, bleeding, weight or growth loss, fever, nocturnal or localised pain, symptoms between attacks.
Abdominal migraine named, with normal tests explained as supporting it.
Dark room, fluids, early paracetamol or ibuprofen per BNFC; diary and triggers.
Antiemetic and triptan restrictions at age 8 respected; paediatric referral for frequent or disabling attacks.
Clear red flags with 999 or A&E routes; face-to-face booked; teach-back.

social.t: Attacks can cause missed school. A short letter explaining the diagnosis and a plan for attacks at school can help.
The mother’s own migraine gives her understanding of triggers and can be used in explanation.

legal.t: Domperidone is licensed only for 12 and over weighing at least 35 kg (MHRA 2019). Off-label use in children is a specialist decision, made with informed consent.

professional.t: Abdominal pain in a child should not be diagnosed without examination; convert to face-to-face when examination is needed.
Repeated tests without a clear question increase anxiety and cost. Explain the rationale for the tests you do order.

community.t: Migraine charities provide information on childhood migraine and its variants, and school health teams can support attendance.

redFlags: Bilious (green) vomiting: possible malrotation or obstruction, emergency
Fever, nocturnal waking, localised or right-sided pain
Symptoms between attacks, dysuria, joint or perianal problems, family history of IBD or coeliac disease
ice: Concern: tests normal but attacks continue

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This fits abdominal migraine: a form of migraine in children that causes attacks of tummy pain rather than headache.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s the same switch in the nervous system that causes your migraines, but in children it often shows up in the tummy. Between attacks the body is completely normal, which is why the tests are normal too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something had been missed because the tests were normal. Normal tests actually fit this diagnosis.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her worry; support school attendance; involve the mother’s migraine experience.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face review: examination, growth chart, urine test
Attacks: dark room, fluids, early paracetamol or ibuprofen per BNFC
Symptom and trigger diary; regular meals, sleep, fluids
Paediatric referral if frequent or disabling
safetyNet: Green vomit or severe unrelenting pain: 999 or A&E
Blood, fever, localised pain, weight loss, unwell between attacks: urgent review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: A telephone case where the diagnosis is recognisable from the history. Marks go to screening alarm features, arranging an examination, explaining why normal tests fit, and treating attacks within licensing.

items.why: Growth, abdominal findings and urine must be checked in a child.

items.fail: Missing bilious vomiting and growth questions.
items.why: Malrotation and organic disease must be excluded.
items.fix: Ask specifically about green vomit, blood, weight and growth.
Rest, fluids and early simple analgesia; paediatric advice if needed.

items.why: Adds anxiety without a clear question.
items.fix: Targeted tests: urine and coeliac serology if not done.

items.fail: “The tests are normal, so it’s nothing.”
items.fix: Explain that normal tests support abdominal migraine.

items.why: Parents need to know which signs are emergencies.
items.fix: Name green vomit, blood, fixed pain, fever and being unwell between attacks, with routes.
